extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of the history of mathematics; readers interested in classical Greek geometric constructions and theory of conics
extracted.subtask_description: Discussion and reconstruction of Greek methods (νεῦσις) for classical construction problems (doubling the cube, trisection of an angle, solving cubics), showing when plane (straightedge-and-compass) methods suffice and when conics or auxiliary analyses are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: General νεῦσις (intercept-by-given-length problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any two straight lines forming an angle and any fixed point not on either line, it is required to draw through the fixed point a straight line such that the portion of it intercepted between the given lines is equal to a given length (the νεῦσις).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the parallelogram on the given angle; introduce an auxiliary point P so that the required intercept corresponds to a chord/segment determined by P; reduce the problem to finding the intersection of (1) a circle with centre at one vertex and radius equal to the given length, and (2) a rectangular hyperbola passing through the opposite vertex and having the parallelogram sides as asymptotes. Intersection yields P, from which the required line is drawn. (This is presented as the 'most general form' of the νεῦσις.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of trisection and doubling-the-cube to the νεῦσις
rubrics_metrics.description: The classical problems of trisecting an arbitrary acute angle and doubling the cube can both be reduced to instances of the νεῦσις (i.e. to drawing through a fixed point a line whose intercepted portion between two given lines equals a given length).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (trisection): form rectangle/parallelogram ABCD, translate the trisection requirement into finding a line through a vertex so that a certain intercept equals a given length; then construct a circle (centre at D, radius k) and a rectangular hyperbola (with specified asymptotes) — their intersection gives the auxiliary point. The same reduction explains Menaechmus' and Apollonius' conic methods for doubling the cube.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plane cases criterion (when νεῦσις is solvable with straightedge and compass)
rubrics_metrics.description: The νεῦσις reduces to a 'plane' (straightedge-and-compass) problem in particular configurations, notably when the fixed point lies on one of the bisectors of the angle between the two given straight lines (i.e., when the constructed parallelogram is a rhombus or a square).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In these special cases the auxiliary rectangular hyperbola degenerates or the geometry admits constructions using only circles and lines; Pappus enumerates such 'plane' cases as especially useful and gives constructions (and lemmas) for the rhombus and square cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heraclitus' square lemma and construction (square case)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a square ABCD, with BHE drawn meeting CD at H and AD produced at E, and EF drawn perpendicular to BE meeting BC produced at F, one has CF^2 = BC^2 + HE^2. Heraclitus uses this to construct the required line when HE (the given length) is specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given HE = k, compute CF from CF^2 = BC^2 + k^2; extend BC to F with CF equal to that value; semicircle on BF as diameter meets AD produced at E; join BE to get the desired line with HE = k. The lemma provides a pure straightedge-and-compass reduction for the square case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apollonius' rhombus construction (plane νεῦσις for a rhombus)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a rhombus/parallelogram special case of the νεῦσις, Apollonius (as restored from Pappus) gives a construction: choose p such that p : k = AB : BC, apply to BC a rectangle exceeding by a square equal to p^2, take BE·EC equal to that rectangle, then with E as centre and radius p describe a circle cutting AC and CD; the resulting points construct the required line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method uses the classical 'application of areas' idea: pick p in proportion to given sides, construct a rectangle equal to p^2 attached to BC, use circle intersections to locate auxiliary points (Κ, H) so that HK equals the given k; joining and producing BK gives the required line. Pappus' proposition is used to justify that the constructed line verges to the correct vertex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conics (parabola and rectangular hyperbola) to solve pure cubic problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure cubic problems (e.g., doubling the cube or extracting cube roots) are solved by constructing two conics whose intersections produce the necessary mean proportionals or linear solution: historically Menaechmus used parabola and hyperbola; Archimedes and Dionysodorus used similar conic intersections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent the required proportional relations by conic equations (e.g., for mean proportionals: a/x = x/y and xy = ab), draw the corresponding parabola and rectangular hyperbola; their intersection points give the mean proportionals and thereby the cube root or doubled-cube construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadratic equations solved by application of areas and mean proportionals
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greeks solved all quadratic equations with positive roots by treating them as relations between areas and transforming rectilineal areas into rectangles and squares; the mean proportional (single) is the basic tool for extracting square roots and for 'multiplying' squares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quadratic problems reduce to finding a mean proportional between two given lengths (geometrically: constructing a line segment whose square equals a given area). Use Euclidean constructions and the Pythagorean theorem (e.g., repeated applications of Euclid I.47) in cases where the area is sum or difference of squares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two mean proportionals method for solving pure cubics
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding two mean proportionals between two given straight lines gives the solution of any pure cubic equation (equivalent to extracting a cube root or effecting the multiplication of the cube by a ratio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If x and y are the two mean proportionals between a and b, then a : x = x : y = y : b, which yields the cube relations needed. Geometric constructions for two mean proportionals (via conics or mechanical devices) therefore solve the cubic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction-to-cubic and need to perform a διορισμός (determine solvability ranges)
rubrics_metrics.description: When problems reduce to cubic equations in general form, one must investigate limits for the possibility of real solutions (διορισμός). For some configurations a real solution exists only if parameters satisfy certain inequalities (e.g., a given length must be at least a minimum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes explicitly investigated the maximum/minimum values determining whether 0, 1, or 2 real roots (between 0 and a) exist for a given cubic reduced from a geometric problem; similarly Pappus examines minimum required lengths in rhombus cases. One must check these constraints before attempting construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedes' method: solve cubic by intersection of specified conics and analyze number of real roots
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes reduced certain geometric division problems to a cubic equation and solved them by intersecting a parabola and a rectangular hyperbola whose equations correspond to the algebraic relation. He also analyzed conditions (διορισμός) giving 0,1, or 2 real roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the cubic in a geometric form (e.g., (a − x)·y^2 = b' with y related to x by conic relation), draw the corresponding conics (parabola and rectangular hyperbola), find their intersections; examine tangency/maximum conditions (e.g., tangency at x = a/3) to determine multiplicity of roots and existence of solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting intersections of conics/circle to determine multiplicity of solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apollonius stresses that studying the possible number of intersection points of conics (or a conic and a circle) is a ready method for observing whether several solutions are possible, that they are so many in number, or that no solution exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geometrical analysis of intersections (including tangency cases) to conclude about the multiplicity and existence of solutions; e.g., rectangular hyperbola intersections with a conic indicate numbers of normals or roots and hence the number of admissible constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical heuristic: special parameter values reveal plane constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek geometers often discovered plane (straightedge-and-compass) special cases by studying special parameter values of the general conic solution — e.g., knowing that a right angle trisection is plane suggested the square case and then the rhombus case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate special values (e.g., given length equal to twice diagonal, or fixed point on bisector) where the general conic configuration simplifies; such special-cases often admit simpler plane constructions and can guide discovery of generalizations.
